item.title: 5.7-magnitude earthquake strikes China
item.description: An earthquake of magnitude 5.7 struck China at a depth of 80 kilometres on Saturday, the National Center for Seismology (NCS) said, reporting another seismic event in the country earlier this month.
item.content:encoded:
5.7-magnitude earthquake strikes China An earthquake of magnitude 5.7 struck China at a depth of 80 kilometres on Saturday, the National Center for Seismology (NCS) said, reporting another seismic event in the country earlier this month. ANI | Updated: 21-11-2026 17:18 IST | Created: 21-11-2026 17:18 IST

Representational Image (File Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

An earthquake of magnitude 5.7 struck China at a depth of 80 kilometres on Saturday, the National Center for Seismology (NCS) said, reporting another seismic event in the country earlier this month. According to the NCS, the earthquake occurred at 4:15:37 pm IST on November 21, at latitude 37.099° North and longitude 96.482° East, with its location reported in China. In a post on X, the National Center for Seismology stated, "EQ of M: 5.7, On: 21/11/2026 16:15:37 IST, Lat: 37.099 N, Long: 96.482 E, Depth: 80 Km, Location: China." The latest earthquake comes after a 4.4-magnitude tremor was recorded in China on November 5. The earlier earthquake occurred at 6:19:17 am IST at a shallow depth of 10 kilometres, with its epicentre at latitude 32.592° North and longitude 94.291° East, according to the NCS. In its post on X, the NCS reported, "EQ of M: 4.4, On: 05/11/2026 06:19:17 IST, Lat: 32.592 N, Long: 94.291 E, Depth: 10 Km, Location: China." The two earthquakes fall into different depth categories under the classification outlined by the United States Geological Survey (USGS). While the November 5 earthquake, at a depth of 10 kilometres, falls in the shallow category, the latest tremor, recorded at 80 kilometres, is classified as an intermediate-depth earthquake. According to the USGS, earthquakes occurring between 0 and 70 kilometres are classified as shallow, those between 70 and 300 kilometres as intermediate, and those between 300 and 700 kilometres as deep earthquakes. The USGS further explains that the term "deep-focus earthquakes" is generally applied to earthquakes occurring at depths greater than 70 kilometres. It also notes that all earthquakes deeper than 70 kilometres are localised within great slabs of lithosphere that are sinking into the Earth's mantle. Explaining the relationship between earthquake depth and surface shaking, the USGS states that "the strength of shaking from an earthquake diminishes with increasing distance from the earthquake's source". It further observes that shaking at the surface from an earthquake occurring at 500 kilometres deep is considerably less than that from an earthquake of the same magnitude occurring at 20 kilometres depth. The USGS also states that earthquakes occur in the crust or upper mantle, which extends from the Earth's surface to about 800 kilometres. (ANI)

item.title: CERT-In flags unauthorised payments beyond financial sector
item.description: The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) has flagged unauthorised payments beyond the financial sector, with reported cases affecting technology service providers that support ...
item.content:encoded:
CERT-In flags unauthorised payments beyond financial sector The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) has flagged unauthorised payments beyond the financial sector, with reported cases affecting technology service providers that support government-linked payments and platforms that handle payouts to vendors and business partners. ANI | Updated: 21-11-2026 15:41 IST | Created: 21-11-2026 15:41 IST

Representative Image (File Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) has flagged unauthorised payments beyond the financial sector, with reported cases affecting technology service providers that support government-linked payments and platforms that handle payouts to vendors and business partners. “CERT-In has received reports of unauthorised financial transactions involving organisations outside the financial sector,” the agency said in an advisory issued on Friday and rated “Critical”. The advisory did not name the affected organisations or disclose the amounts involved. CERT-In said attackers altered business records or approval arrangements that determine who gets paid and then used the regular payment process to make unauthorised transactions. That meant a payment could clear routine checks even when the information behind it had been tampered with. “A transaction may pass the usual application and approval checks even when the records used to initiate it have been changed without authorisation,” the advisory said. The agency urged government organisations and other entities that rely on technology service providers to check payment instructions and key records against independent sources. It also called for independent verification of changes to payment instructions, beneficiaries and approval arrangements. CERT-In said multiple approvals within the same provider’s system may offer limited protection if that system has been compromised. The warning follows CERT-In’s October 9 advisory on unauthorised fund transfers involving banks and other financial services firms and its November 4 update on AI-driven attacks targeting the sector. The latest advisory also asks technology providers and payout platforms to keep clients’ systems separate and monitor changes to payment records alongside approvals and subsequent transactions. In separate investigations, CERT-In identified the use of AI-driven tools in cyberattacks targeting businesses, technology and other service providers, government organisations, and academic and research institutions. It said these tools can shorten the time between identifying a target and launching subsequent stages of an attack. CERT-In reiterated that organisations must report incidents covered by its April 2022 directions within six hours of discovering them or being informed of them. It said cases involving unauthorised financial transactions should also be reported promptly through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal or by calling 1930. (ANI)

item.title: Iran-US negotiations stalled over uranium enrichment dispute, mediators warn of renewed conflict: Report
item.description: Negotiations between the United States and Iran have stalled over disagreements concerning Tehran's enriched uranium stockpile, with mediators warning that they cannot guarantee a return to military ...
item.content:encoded:
Iran-US negotiations stalled over uranium enrichment dispute, mediators warn of renewed conflict: Report Negotiations between the United States and Iran have stalled over disagreements concerning Tehran's enriched uranium stockpile, with mediators warning that they cannot guarantee a return to military escalation in the Middle East. ANI | Updated: 21-11-2026 14:49 IST | Created: 21-11-2026 14:49 IST

Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei (Photo: x/@Rahbarenghelab_) and US President Donald Trump (File Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

Country:

Iran

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Negotiations between the United States and Iran have stalled over disagreements concerning Tehran's enriched uranium stockpile, with mediators warning that they cannot guarantee a return to military escalation in the Middle East. Washington is insisting on a clear roadmap and written guarantees from Iran that it will eliminate its enriched uranium stockpile and refrain from resuming uranium enrichment in the future, Al Arabiya English reported, citing a senior source. However, both sides have maintained firm positions on the issue despite several proposals put forward by mediators to bridge their differences, the report said. The diplomatic deadlock comes amid continuing tensions between Washington and Tehran, with both countries yet to reach an understanding on the future of Iran's nuclear programme. Earlier, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran would not accept an agreement with Washington merely to end the current diplomatic impasse, insisting that any settlement must protect Iran's national interests and provide assurances against another military confrontation. In an interview with an Iranian state-run newspaper, as reported by Al Jazeera, Araghchi said Iran was seeking a "good, honourable and lasting agreement" rather than remaining in a situation of "neither war nor peace". Questioning the durability of any potential understanding with Washington, he said, "What is the point of reaching an agreement today if it is violated two months later and war resumes?" Araghchi recalled that fighting had resumed just 15 days after the June ceasefire agreement, arguing that Tehran would not accept an arrangement simply to escape the current situation. On the nuclear issue, the Iranian Foreign Minister said Tehran was open to negotiations over its stockpile of uranium enriched to 60 per cent but ruled out transferring the material outside the country. He maintained that a fair formula could be reached on uranium enrichment, provided it formed part of a broader agreement addressing Iran's national interests and security concerns. Araghchi also confirmed that Tehran and Washington continued exchanging messages and proposals through mediators, including Qatar and Pakistan. "We are people of diplomacy, and we still have hope in diplomacy," he said. Meanwhile, he maintained that Iran remained willing to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if Washington fulfilled its conditions, underlining Tehran's position that any diplomatic settlement must address its nuclear programme, sanctions and security concerns. (ANI)
